prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints interact with asset prices to amplify and propagate shocks, and for the resulting theory of credit cycles

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed from B032 (Persson, Tabellini, Besley) to B003 (Kiyotaki, Moore). In round 1 I ranked B003 second and called it one of the strongest cases on the shortlist. After the exchange, I think it beats my own B032 case on the common criteria. Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) give one identifiable mechanism: borrowing limits tied to collateral value, together with durable-asset prices that respond to those limits, turn small shocks into large and persistent fluctuations. The credit is the cleanest on the shortlist, and no round-1 file argues for restoring Gertler. The work is about three decades old and was tested by 2008 and the quantitative macro-finance literature that followed, so maturity is not a problem. The 2022 overlap is the main objection, and I find Strömberg's and Teorell's answer persuasive. That prize concerned banks as intermediaries, bank runs and the Depression-era credit channel. Kiyotaki-Moore concerns borrowers' collateral and the dynamics of asset prices, so it is a different discovery. I handle the remaining overlap risk through drafting: the citation names the collateral-constraint mechanism and does not refer to financial crises in general. My reasons for moving off B032 are the ones I recorded myself. The 2024 institutions prize is a recent neighbour. The cross-country constitutional estimates have identification limits. Besley's place alongside the other two is unsettled. I am also working outside my field there. None of these is fatal, but B003 is stronger on attribution and on how well the mechanism has held up. I do not move because B014 has six stated preferences. Those counts are not evidence of merit, and I still do not rank B014 first.
statement.case_against: The first reservation is the 2022 prize. If the committee reads the credit-cycle mechanism as part of the territory already honoured, the marginal case weakens, and drafting can only partly fix that. Second, the original paper is a theory paper. Hjalmarsson, Teorell and Strömberg all note that direct identification of the collateral channel came mostly from later work, and as an applied microeconometrician I count that as a real cost. The quantitative importance of collateral constraints relative to other financial frictions is still debated. Third, B014 has a much larger footprint in central-bank practice, and Strömberg and Teorell concede that. If the committee decides that breadth of policy influence is decisive and that a narrowly worded Calvo-Taylor-Woodford citation is defensible, B014 could rightly outrank B003. Fourth, a pair is a narrow award, and it may be seen as thin compared with the broad literature it inspired. I am not independently verifying priority or attribution claims.

responses.point: Strömberg prefers the Kiyotaki-Moore pair, having dropped Gertler. He argues that collateral-driven amplification differs from the banks-and-crises work recognised in 2022, and that B014 would only be preferable if a narrower, defensible citation can be found.
responses.response: I agree on the pair and on the distinction from 2022, and this is a main reason I moved to B003. I would sharpen your concession on B014. Its larger policy footprint is real, but a larger footprint does not settle what is being credited. You are right that the pricing friction, the policy rule and the synthesis are different discoveries. I would still not make a prize turn on the 2022 point alone. Your better argument is that the mechanism is the template for later macro-finance models, and I would keep the case on that.

responses.point: Teorell prefers B003 and keeps the pair. He treats the 2022 overlap as a drafting problem, and he discloses a co-authored paper with Persson that is the reason B032 is only his alternative.
responses.response: I agree that the overlap is a matter of wording: the citation should name collateral constraints and asset-price feedback, not financial crises. Your disclosure and your remark on identification in the constitutional studies also fed into my move. I had already conceded that identification point in round 1. In the exchange, no one else argued for B032 on the merits, and I could not rebut my own reservations strongly enough to keep it first. I also accept your point that the original paper is theoretical. I would answer it by saying the mechanism has since been quantified and extended in a large literature, though I treat this as a cost and not a settled question.

responses.point: Krusell prefers B014 with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. He regards the nominal-rigidity and policy-rule core as the one paradigm that changed both academic modelling and daily policy, and he sees the 2022 prize as narrowing B003's marginal room. He accepts that excluding Galí, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets is a real cost.
responses.response: I accept that B014 has the broadest practical influence and I keep it as my first alternative. I part ways on whether influence settles the matter. I work on firm price-setting, and the micro evidence on price adjustment shows that time-dependent rules such as Calvo's are a convenient approximation, not a description of how firms set prices. State-dependent menu-cost behaviour has different aggregate implications. This does not make Calvo's device unimportant. Influence and tractability are what count for a prize, and the device is the primitive of the New Keynesian Phillips curve. It does bear on Fredriksson's question of whether it is a discovery in the sense the committee usually rewards, and it makes me prefer a prize with a mechanism that does not depend on that debate. On 2022, I read your concern as a real one that drafting can reduce, and I do not think it leaves B003 without room.

responses.point: As chair, Hassler prefers B014, regards B003 as a clean two-person attribution, and doubts that the marginal gain from recognising collateral-constraint dynamics outweighs recognising the monetary-policy framework after the 2022 prize. He asks why the mechanism deserves priority now.
responses.response: My answer rests on three criteria and not on counts. The first is attribution clarity: B003 is a single mechanism with two originators, while B014 requires choosing among several with claims, which every B014 supporter records as the main weakness. The second is marginal distinctiveness: the 2022 prize covered banks, runs and the Depression-era credit channel, not borrower collateral and asset-price amplification. The third is durability: the mechanism has survived 2008 and the quantitative work after it. I would change my ordering in two cases. One is a majority view that the 2022 prize covers this ground. The other is a citation for B014 that credits specific discoveries without implying a ranking of the excluded contributors. In either case B014 would become my first choice, and I would vote for Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. I note that I co-authored the 2026 IJIO paper with you and Ellingsen. That tie covers a price-adjustment topic close to B014, and I disclose it here.

responses.point: Fredriksson prefers B014 and asks whether Calvo's compact pricing device is a discovery in the sense the committee usually rewards. He also wants wording that does not claim the estimated-DSGE tradition.
responses.response: I think your question is the right one, and it is the one the chair's questions leave open. If the committee answers yes, the wording you ask for, naming the pricing friction, the rule and the synthesis without claiming the estimated tradition, is the most defensible B014 framing. I would still need to see agreement on that, and I do not see it in the round-1 files. Hjalmarsson and Hassler would accept Galí in place of Calvo, and Andersson says the Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans claim is not derivative. B003 does not face an unresolved question about which discovery is being credited.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the 2022 prize as covering the collateral-constraint mechanism, and whether wording that names collateral constraints and asset-price feedback is enough to separate the two.
How much weight the theoretical character of the 1997 paper, with identification coming mostly from later work, should carry compared with B014's decades of policy use.

Whether B014 can be given a citation that credits Calvo, Taylor and Woodford for specific discoveries without implying a ranking of Galí, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Evans, Smets, Wouters and Gertler. If it can, I would reconsider.
Whether my move reflects the common criteria or familiarity with a pair that is easy to evaluate from outside macro. I work in IO and trade, so I cannot rule this out.
I have not independently verified priority, attribution or the empirical record from outside the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: No recusal-level connection to Kiyotaki, Moore or any other shortlisted candidate is apparent from my supplied profile. B032 is no longer in my preferred configuration. For transparency, the profile records public facts that I do not treat as bearing on any candidate. I co-authored with committee chair John Hassler and former chair Tore Ellingsen (IJIO 2026) on price adjustment. That topic is thematically close to B014, where Hassler is a supporter. I am married to Magdalena Andersson, which is a public fact only. I am at the Stockholm School of Economics in Stockholm, which is the same city as several committee colleagues and as Persson's university, but I have no personal or co-authorship link to Persson, Tabellini or Besley. Disclosed only; not adjudicated.
